description: Continuous, fartlek, interval, circuit, weight, plyometric and HIIT training methods matched to fitness aims.
content_html:
Why Choose the Right Training Method?

Not all training is created equal. A marathon runner who only does heavy weight training will not improve her aerobic endurance; a sprinter who only plods along at a slow jog will never develop the explosive power he needs off the blocks. Training must be specific to the demands of the sport — this is the principle of specificity in action. Choosing the correct training method is therefore the first and most important decision a coach or athlete makes when designing a programme. OCR identifies seven training methods you need to know: continuous, fartlek, interval, circuit, weight, plyometric and HIIT.

Continuous Training

Continuous training involves exercising at a steady pace for a minimum of 20 minutes without any rest breaks. Activities such as running, cycling, swimming and rowing are all commonly used. Because the intensity remains constant and the body has a continuous oxygen supply, continuous training primarily develops cardiovascular endurance. It is well suited to distance runners, rowers and cyclists.

The main advantage is that it is simple, low-cost and easy to monitor — a runner simply keeps going at a steady pace within their aerobic training zone (60–80% of maximum heart rate). A disadvantage is that it can become repetitive and may not replicate the varied demands of team sports, which involve bursts of speed interspersed with periods of lower intensity.

Fartlek Training

Fartlek training takes its name from the Swedish for “speed play.” Unlike standard continuous training, fartlek deliberately mixes periods of higher intensity effort with periods of slower recovery running, all without stopping. A footballer might jog steadily for two minutes, then sprint for 30 seconds, then stride at half-pace for a minute, then repeat. Because the performer decides when to change pace, it replicates the unpredictable demands of many team sports.

Key Fact

Fartlek means “speed play” in Swedish. It varies speed and terrain continuously, making it ideal for team-sport athletes whose games combine aerobic and anaerobic demands — such as footballers, rugby players and hockey players.

Interval Training

Interval training uses a planned work:rest ratio — a set period of hard effort followed by a set period of rest or low-intensity recovery. The athlete repeats this pattern for a fixed number of sets. For example, a 400 m track athlete might run 200 m at race pace, rest for 90 seconds, and repeat six times. By controlling the work:rest ratio, the coach can target either aerobic or anaerobic systems: longer work periods with short rests challenge the aerobic system, while very short, maximal sprints with longer rests target the anaerobic system.

Many students assume interval training is always anaerobic because of the repeated high-intensity efforts. In fact, the energy system targeted depends entirely on the work:rest ratio and intensity. A 3-minute effort at 65% maximum heart rate, with 1 minute of walking recovery, repeated five times, is aerobic interval training. Anaerobic interval training requires efforts above 80% of maximum heart rate with longer recovery periods. Always identify the intensity and duration to justify which energy system is being stressed — this is exactly the justification the mark scheme looks for.

HIIT

HIIT (High Intensity Interval Training) is a specific form of interval training where the work periods are performed at near-maximal intensity — typically above 80% of maximum heart rate, within the anaerobic training zone — and rest periods are short. A typical HIIT session might involve 20 seconds of all-out effort followed by 10 seconds of rest, repeated eight times. HIIT is time-efficient and produces improvements in both aerobic capacity and anaerobic power, making it popular with athletes who are pressed for time.

Circuit Training

Circuit training involves moving around a series of stations, performing a specific exercise at each one before moving on to the next. A coach designing a circuit must consider: the space and equipment available, the number of stations, the work:rest ratio at each station, and the type of exercise at each station. The beauty of circuit training is its flexibility — by changing the exercises, the number of stations, the time at each station and the rest periods, the same circuit format can be adapted to develop cardiovascular endurance, muscular endurance, strength or power.

For example, a muscular endurance circuit might include press-ups, sit-ups, squat jumps, tricep dips and step-ups, each performed for 45 seconds with 15 seconds to move to the next station. To make the same circuit develop strength instead, the coach would add resistance (using dumbbells or weighted vests), reduce the repetitions per station and increase the rest periods.

Weight Training

Weight training uses free weights, machines or bodyweight exercises with added resistance to develop muscular strength, power or muscular endurance. The fitness aim determines the weight and repetitions used. For strength and power, athletes use a high weight (above 70% of one rep max) and a low number of repetitions — approximately three sets of four to eight repetitions. For muscular endurance, athletes use a lower weight (below 70% of one rep max) with a high number of repetitions — approximately three sets of 12 to 15 repetitions.

Safe practice is non-negotiable: correct lifting technique prevents injury, appropriate weight selection avoids overloading, and a spotter should be present when performing heavy lifts such as the bench press or squat. The back should remain straight during deadlifts and squats to protect the lumbar vertebrae.

Key Fact

Strength/power training: above 70% of one rep max, approximately 3 sets of 4–8 reps. Muscular endurance training: below 70% of one rep max, approximately 3 sets of 12–15 reps. The fitness aim determines the weight and rep range.

Plyometric Training

Plyometric training develops explosive power. The physiological basis is the stretch-shortening cycle: the muscle first undergoes a rapid lengthening phase as the athlete lands or prepares, storing elastic energy in the muscle and tendon; this is immediately followed by a powerful shortening contraction as the athlete jumps, bounds or throws. The faster the transition between these two phases, the greater the power output. Exercises include bounding, depth jumping, box jumps and medicine-ball throws. Plyometrics is well suited to sprinters, high jumpers, basketball players and volleyball players — any athlete who needs explosive leg or upper-body power.

Consider a county-level basketball player with a 10-week pre-season. Her coach wants to improve cardiovascular endurance, muscular power and agility. An appropriate programme might combine: (1) fartlek training twice a week to mirror the stop-start aerobic and anaerobic demands of a basketball game; (2) plyometric training twice a week (depth jumps and bounding) to improve explosive jumping power for rebounds and lay-ups; (3) HIIT sessions to raise anaerobic threshold and improve the player’s ability to sustain high-intensity efforts late in the fourth quarter. Continuous training alone would be insufficient because it would not develop the anaerobic power the sport demands.
exam_tip_html: On a “6-mark Analyse” question about training methods, the most common error is producing a one-sided answer — for example, only listing advantages of a method without weighing its disadvantages or comparing it to an alternative. Each point should be developed: name the method, describe what it does, link it to a sporting context. Use a “For X… However Y…” structure and anchor every point to a named sport or athlete type. For 2-mark “State Two” questions, make sure your two answers are genuinely different — saying “it improves aerobic fitness” and “it improves cardiovascular endurance” is the same point and will only earn one mark. Remember: OCR lists HIIT as a separate named training method, not just as a category of interval training.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Each training method has a primary fitness focus: continuous and fartlek develop cardiovascular endurance; interval and HIIT target aerobic and anaerobic capacity depending on the work:rest ratio; weight training develops strength or muscular endurance depending on the load and rep range; plyometrics develops explosive power.
  • The work:rest ratio is the key variable in interval and circuit training — shorter rests and longer work periods stress the aerobic system, while shorter work periods at maximal intensity with longer rests stress the anaerobic system.
  • Training must always be matched to the demands of the sport (specificity) and the fitness aim of the athlete. Evaluating a method means weighing its advantages and disadvantages in the context of a specific sport and performer.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes HIIT?
A) Sustained exercise at a constant pace for at least 20 minutes
B) Short bursts of near-maximal effort alternated with brief rest periods
C) Moving around a series of exercise stations with different fitness aims
D) Explosive bounding movements to develop muscular power
practice_questions.marks: B) Short bursts of near-maximal effort alternated with brief rest periods [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: State two advantages of circuit training compared to continuous training.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each of two distinct advantages, for example: It can target multiple components of fitness in one session (1); it can be adapted by changing stations, rest periods or resistance (1); it can replicate sport-specific movements (1); it provides variety, which supports motivation (1). Responses must be qualitatively different to earn both marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe how plyometric training develops muscular power.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: the muscle undergoes a rapid lengthening phase first (1); elastic energy is stored in the muscle and tendon during this phase (1); this is immediately followed by a powerful shortening contraction (1); the rapid transition between phases (the stretch-shortening cycle) produces a greater power output than a concentric contraction alone (1). Any three of the above, clearly described.

practice_questions.text: Explain why fartlek training is more appropriate for a football player than continuous training.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: fartlek varies speed and intensity throughout the session, including bursts of high-intensity effort (1); this mirrors the intermittent demands of football, where players alternate between jogging, sprinting and walking (1); continuous training maintains a steady pace and develops aerobic endurance only (1); football requires both aerobic and anaerobic capacity, and fartlek training stresses both energy systems (1). Full marks require both an explanation of what fartlek does AND why this is more appropriate for football than continuous training.

practice_questions.text: A 17-year-old club-level long jumper wants to increase her explosive leg power over a 12-week training block. Analyse the use of plyometric training and weight training as methods she could use to achieve this goal.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (5–6 marks): balanced analysis of both methods. Identifies advantages of plyometrics (replicates the stretch-shortening cycle of the take-off, develops power quickly, sport-specific) and limitations (high injury risk if technique is poor, requires strength base). Identifies advantages of weight training (builds the muscular strength base that underpins power; load and rep ranges can be adjusted; low injury risk with correct technique) and limitations (less sport-specific than plyometrics; muscular hypertrophy may not directly translate to explosive power). Applies both methods specifically to long jump demands. May recommend a combination. Uses accurate terminology throughout.

Secure (3–4 marks): discusses both methods with some application to long jump; advantages and limitations present for at least one method; generally accurate.

Developing (2 marks): relevant points about one method; limited sporting application.

Emerging (1 mark): names one method with minimal development.

practice_questions.text: A sprint coach is designing an interval training session for a 100 m sprinter. Explain how the work:rest ratio should be set to ensure the anaerobic energy system is targeted, and why this is important for the sprinter's performance.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 4 marks: the work period should be short and at maximal intensity (above 80% max HR / all-out sprint) (1); the rest period should be longer than the work period to allow anaerobic energy stores to partially recover (1); for example, a 10-second maximal sprint followed by 50–60 seconds of rest would target the anaerobic system (1); this is important because a 100 m sprint is entirely anaerobic — the race lasts under 12 seconds and the intensity is too high for aerobic respiration to meet the energy demand (1).

knowledge_checks.q: Which training method involves moving around a series of exercise stations in sequence?
For muscular endurance training, which of the following describes the correct weight and rep range?
options: Above 70% of one rep max, 4–8 reps
Above 80% of one rep max, 2–4 reps
Below 70% of one rep max, 12–15 reps
Below 50% of one rep max, 6–10 reps

knowledge_checks.q: Plyometric training develops power through a rapid lengthening phase followed immediately by a powerful _____ contraction.
In interval training, the _____ ratio describes the relationship between the exercise period and the rest period.
Match each training method to its primary fitness benefit.

flashcard_questions.a: Sustained aerobic exercise at a constant pace, without rest, for at least 20 minutes.
Speed play — it is the Swedish term for a training method that mixes varying intensities without stopping.

flashcard_questions.q: In interval training, what does the work:rest ratio control?
flashcard_questions.a: The balance between effort and recovery, determining which energy system is targeted.

flashcard_questions.q: What weight and rep range is used for strength and power in weight training?
flashcard_questions.a: Above 70% of one rep max, approximately 3 sets of 4–8 reps.

flashcard_questions.q: What weight and rep range is used for muscular endurance in weight training?
flashcard_questions.a: Below 70% of one rep max, approximately 3 sets of 12–15 reps.

flashcard_questions.q: What physiological mechanism does plyometric training exploit?
flashcard_questions.a: The stretch-shortening cycle: rapid lengthening stores elastic energy, then the shortening contraction releases it.
High-intensity interval training: near-maximal effort bursts alternated with short rest periods.

flashcard_questions.q: Name two variables a coach adjusts to change the fitness aim of a circuit.
flashcard_questions.a: Any two of: number of stations, time per station, rest period, exercise type, resistance.

flashcard_questions.q: Why must a spotter be present during heavy weight training lifts?
flashcard_questions.a: To assist or catch the barbell if the performer fails the lift, preventing injury.

flashcard_questions.q: Which training method is most closely matched to the intermittent demands of team sports like football?
flashcard_questions.a: Fartlek training, because it mixes varying speeds and intensities without stopping.

flashcard_questions.q: How does HIIT differ from standard interval training?
flashcard_questions.a: HIIT uses near-maximal intensity work periods (above 80% max HR) and very short rest periods.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the primary fitness component developed by plyometric training?

glossary_terms.definition: A structured programme of exercise designed to improve one or more components of fitness.
Sustained aerobic exercise at a constant pace without rest periods, lasting at least 20 minutes.
A form of continuous training that varies speed, terrain and work-to-recovery ratios throughout the session.
A structured training method alternating periods of high-intensity exercise with timed rest or low-intensity recovery periods.
The ratio of exercise time to rest time in an interval session, for example 1:2 meaning one minute of work to two minutes of rest.
A training method consisting of a series of exercises or stations performed in sequence, with each station targeting a different component of fitness or body area.
A training method using rapid, explosive movements such as bounding and depth jumping to develop muscular power through a rapid stretch of the muscle followed by a powerful contraction.
High-intensity interval training: a form of interval training in which work periods are performed at near-maximal intensity and rest periods are short.

hero_image_caption: Selecting the right training method — from continuous running to plyometric bounding — ensures fitness gains match sport demands.
